quals-wisconsin-algebra-2011f-01.title: Normal $p$-complements are characteristic
quals-wisconsin-algebra-2011f-01.body:
Let $K$ be a normal $p$-complement of $G$.

**(a)** $H\cap K\trianglelefteq H$, $|H\cap K|$ divides $|K|$ so $p\nmid|H\cap K|$, and $|H:H\cap K|=|HK:K|$ divides $|G:K|$, a power of $p$. So $H\cap K$ is a normal $p$-complement of $H$.

**(b)** $KN/N\trianglelefteq G/N$; $|KN/N|=|K:K\cap N|$ divides $|K|$, so it is prime to $p$; and $|G/N:KN/N|=|G:KN|$ divides $|G:K|$, a power of $p$.

**(c)** *Claim: a normal $p$-complement $K$ of a group $X$ is the set of all $p'$-elements of $X$; in particular it is unique and characteristic in $X$.* Elements of $K$ have order dividing $|K|$, prime to $p$. Conversely if $x\in X$ has order prime to $p$, the order of $xK$ in the $p$-group $X/K$ divides both a power of $p$ and the order of $x$, so it is $1$ and $x\in K$.

Let $K_U,K_V$ be the normal $p$-complements of $U,V$. Being characteristic in the normal subgroups $U,V$, they are normal in $G$. Put $K=K_UK_V\trianglelefteq G$; $|K|=|K_U||K_V|/|K_U\cap K_V|$ is prime to $p$, and $K\le UV$, $K\trianglelefteq UV$. In $UV/K$, the subgroups $UK/K\cong U/(U\cap K)$ and $VK/K$ are $p$-groups (quotients of $U/K_U$ and $V/K_V$ respectively, as $K_U\le U\cap K$) and normal. Hence $UV/K=(UK/K)(VK/K)$ has order $|UK/K||VK/K|/|UK/K\cap VK/K|$, a power of $p$. Thus $K$ is a normal $p$-complement of $UV$. ∎

quals-wisconsin-algebra-2011f-02.title: Colon ideals of a primary ideal
quals-wisconsin-algebra-2011f-02.body:
Let $P=\sqrt Q$, a prime ideal.

**(a)** $Q\subseteq I$ (as $Q$ is an ideal), so $\sqrt Q\subseteq\sqrt I$. If $r\in\sqrt I$ then $r^k\in I$, i.e. $a\,r^k\in Q$; since $a\notin Q$ and $Q$ is primary, some power of $r^k$ lies in $Q$, so $r\in\sqrt Q$.

**(b)** $1\notin I$ since $a\notin Q$, so $I$ is proper. Let $xy\in I$ with $x\notin I$. Then $(ax)y\in Q$ and $ax\notin Q$, so $y^k\in Q\subseteq I$ for some $k$. Hence $I$ is primary.

**(c)** *First proof.* The family $\{(Q:a)\mid a\in R\setminus Q\}$ is nonempty ($a=1$ gives $Q$) and consists of proper ideals. As $R$ is noetherian it has a maximal member $I=(Q:a)$. Let $xy\in I$ with $x\notin I$. Then $ax\notin Q$, and $(Q:ax)\supseteq(Q:a)=I$, so by maximality $(Q:ax)=I$. Since $axy\in Q$, $y\in(Q:ax)=I$. Thus $I$ is prime.

*Second proof.* $P$ is finitely generated, so $P^N\subseteq Q$ for some $N$ (a power of each generator lies in $Q$). Let $k\ge1$ be minimal with $P^k\subseteq Q$ ($P^0=R\not\subseteq Q$), and pick $a\in P^{k-1}\setminus Q$. Then $aP\subseteq P^k\subseteq Q$, so $P\subseteq I$, while $I\subseteq\sqrt I=P$ by (a). Hence $I=P$ is prime. ∎

quals-wisconsin-algebra-2011f-03.title: Kummer theory and natural irrationalities
quals-wisconsin-algebra-2011f-03.body:
Let $\zeta\in K$ be a primitive $n$th root of unity; then $\operatorname{char}K\nmid n$ (otherwise $X^n-1$ would have fewer than $n$ distinct roots).

**(a)** If $\alpha=0$ then $E=F$, $L\subseteq F$, so $L=L\cap F=K=K[1]$. Let $c=\alpha^n\ne0$. The roots of $X^n-c$ are $\zeta^i\alpha\in E$ and are distinct, so $E$ is the splitting field over $F$ of the separable polynomial $X^n-c$; thus $E/F$ is Galois. For $\sigma\in\mathrm{Gal}(E/F)$, $\sigma(\alpha)=\omega_\sigma\alpha$ with $\omega_\sigma^n=1$, and $\sigma\mapsto\omega_\sigma$ is an injective homomorphism into $\langle\zeta\rangle$ (as $\zeta$ is fixed and $\alpha$ generates $E$). So $\mathrm{Gal}(E/F)$ is cyclic of order dividing $n$.

Since $L/K$ is finite Galois, the theorem on natural irrationalities says $LF/F$ is Galois and restriction gives $\mathrm{Gal}(LF/F)\cong\mathrm{Gal}(L/L\cap F)=\mathrm{Gal}(L/K)$. As $F\subseteq LF\subseteq E$, $\mathrm{Gal}(LF/F)$ is a quotient of the cyclic group $\mathrm{Gal}(E/F)$. Hence $\mathrm{Gal}(L/K)$ is cyclic of some order $m\mid n$.

$K$ contains the primitive $m$th root of unity $\zeta^{n/m}$ and $\operatorname{char}K\nmid m$, so by Kummer theory (Hilbert's Theorem 90) a cyclic extension of degree $m$ has the form $L=K(\beta)$ with $\beta^m\in K$. Then $\beta^n=(\beta^m)^{n/m}\in K$.

**(b)** Take $n=2$ (so the primitive square root $-1$ lies in every field of characteristic $\neq 2$), $K=\mathbb Q$, $\theta=\sqrt[3]2$, $\omega=e^{2\pi i/3}$, and
$$F=\mathbb Q(\omega\theta),\qquad \alpha=\sqrt{-3},\qquad E=F[\alpha],\qquad L=\mathbb Q(\theta).$$
Then $\alpha^2=-3\in F$. Since $\omega=(-1+\sqrt{-3})/2\in E$, $E=\mathbb Q(\omega\theta,\omega)=\mathbb Q(\theta,\omega)$, the splitting field of $X^3-2$, so $L\subseteq E$. $L$ and $F$ are distinct subfields of degree $3$ over $\mathbb Q$ ($L\subseteq\mathbb R$, $F\not\subseteq\mathbb R$), so $L\cap F$ has degree dividing $3$ and less than $3$: $L\cap F=\mathbb Q=K$. But $L=\mathbb Q(\sqrt[3]2)$ is not Galois over $\mathbb Q$: it contains only one root of the irreducible polynomial $X^3-2$. ∎

quals-wisconsin-algebra-2011f-04.title: Values on basis vectors
quals-wisconsin-algebra-2011f-04.body:
**(a)** With pointwise operations, $(f+g)(x)=f(x)+g(x)$ and $(cf)(x)=cf(x)$, sums and scalar multiples of multilinear alternating functions are again multilinear and alternating, and the zero function lies in $S$; so $S$ is a subspace of the vector space of all functions $V^m\to K$.

Two consequences of the definition, for $f\in S$:
1. *Antisymmetry.* Expanding $0=f(\dots,x+y,\dots,x+y,\dots)$ (positions $i,j$) by linearity and discarding the two terms with a repeated argument gives $f(\dots,x,\dots,y,\dots)=-f(\dots,y,\dots,x,\dots)$. Hence permuting the arguments by $\pi$ multiplies $f$ by $\operatorname{sgn}\pi$.
2. *Dependent tuples.* If $x_j=\sum_{i\ne j}c_ix_i$, then expanding in the $j$th slot writes $f(x_1,\dots,x_m)$ as a sum of terms each with a repeated argument, so it is $0$.

If $m>n$, any $m$ vectors in $V$ are linearly dependent, so $f=0$ by 2. Hence $S=0$.

**(b)** Let $e_1,\dots,e_n$ be a basis. Writing $x_k=\sum_ia_{ki}e_i$ and expanding by multilinearity,
$$f(x_1,\dots,x_m)=\sum_{i_1,\dots,i_m}a_{1i_1}\cdots a_{mi_m}\,f(e_{i_1},\dots,e_{i_m}).$$
Terms with a repeated index vanish, and by antisymmetry each remaining $f(e_{i_1},\dots,e_{i_m})$ is $\pm f(e_{j_1},\dots,e_{j_m})$ with $j_1<\dots<j_m$ the sorted indices. So $f$ is determined by the $\binom nm$ values $f(e_J)$, $J=\{j_1<\dots<j_m\}$. The linear map $S\to K^{\binom nm}$, $f\mapsto(f(e_J))_J$, is therefore injective, and $\dim_KS\le\binom nm$.

For $m=n$ this gives $\dim S\le1$. The determinant $D(x_1,\dots,x_n)=\det[a_{ki}]$ of the coordinate matrix is multilinear and alternating (a matrix with two equal rows has determinant $0$) and $D(e_1,\dots,e_n)=1$, so $D\neq0$ and $\dim_KS=1$. ∎
